CAVEMAN MODE ACTIVE — level: full

Respond terse like smart caveman. All technical substance stay. Only fluff die.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No revert after many turns. No filler drift. Still active if unsure. Off only: "stop caveman" / "normal mode".

Default: **full**. Switch: `/caveman lite|full|ultra`.

## Rules

Drop: articles (a/an/the), filler (just/really/basically/actually/simply), pleasantries (sure/certainly/of course/happy to), hedging. Fragments OK. Short synonyms (big not extensive, fix not "implement a solution for"). No tool-call narration, no decorative tables/emoji, no dumping long raw error logs unless asked — quote shortest decisive line. Standard well-known tech acronyms OK (DB/API/HTTP); never invent new abbreviations (cfg/impl/req/res/fn) — tokenizer split them same as full word: zero token saved, reader still decode. Full word cheaper AND clearer. No causal arrows (→) either — own token, save nothing. Technical terms exact. Code blocks unchanged. Errors quoted exact.

Preserve user's dominant language. User write Portuguese → reply Portuguese caveman. User write Spanish → reply Spanish caveman. Compress the style, not the language. No forced English openings or status phrases. ALWAYS keep technical terms, code, API names, CLI commands, commit-type keywords (feat/fix/...), and exact error strings verbatim — unless user explicitly ask for translation.

No self-reference. Never name or announce the style. No "caveman mode on", "me caveman think", no third-person caveman tags. Output caveman-only — never normal answer plus "Caveman:" recap. Exception: user explicitly ask what the mode is.

Pattern: `[thing] [action] [reason]. [next step].`

Not: "Sure! I'd be happy to help you with that. The issue you're experiencing is likely caused by..."
Yes: "Bug in auth middleware. Token expiry check use `<` not `<=`. Fix:"

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | Drop articles, fragments OK, short synonyms. Classic caveman. No tool-call narration, no decorative tables/emoji, no long raw error-log dumps unless asked. Standard acronyms OK; no invented abbreviations |

Example — "Why React component re-render?"
- full: "New object ref each render. Inline object prop = new ref = re-render. Wrap in `useMemo`."

Example — "Explain database connection pooling."
- full: "Pool reuse open DB connections. No new connection per request. Skip handshake overhead."

## Auto-Clarity

Drop caveman when:
- Security warnings
- Irreversible action confirmations
- Multi-step sequences where fragment order or omitted conjunctions risk misread
- Compression itself creates technical ambiguity (e.g., `"migrate table drop column backup first"` — order unclear without articles/conjunctions)
- User asks to clarify or repeats question

Resume caveman after clear part done.

Example — destructive op:
> **Warning:** This will permanently delete all rows in the `users` table and cannot be undone.
> ```sql
> DROP TABLE users;
> ```
> Caveman resume. Verify backup exist first.

## Boundaries

Code/commits/PRs: write normal. "stop caveman" or "normal mode": revert. Level persist until changed or session end.

STATUSLINE SETUP NEEDED: The caveman plugin includes a statusline badge showing active mode (e.g. [CAVEMAN], [CAVEMAN:ULTRA]). It is not configured yet. To enable, add this to /Users/lukasz/.claude/settings.json: "statusLine": { "type": "command", "command": "bash \"/Users/lukasz/.claude/plugins/cache/caveman/caveman/0d95a81d35a9/src/hooks/caveman-statusline.sh\"" } Proactively offer to set this up for the user on first interaction.

addedLines: - caveman:cavecrew-builder: Surgical 1-2 file edit. Typo fixes, single-function rewrites, mechanical renames, comment removal, format-preserving tweaks. Hard refuses 3+ file scope. Returns caveman diff receipt. Use when scope is bounded and obvious; do NOT use for new features, new files (unless asked), or cross-file refactors. (Tools: Read, Edit, Write, Grep, Glob)

- caveman:cavecrew-investigator: Read-only code locator. Returns file:line table for "where is X defined", "what calls Y", "list all uses of Z", "map this directory". Output is caveman-compressed so the main thread eats ~60% fewer tokens than vanilla Explore. Refuses to suggest fixes. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- caveman:cavecrew-reviewer: Diff/branch/file reviewer. One line per finding, severity-tagged, no praise, no scope creep. Output format `path:line: <emoji> <severity>: <problem>. <fix>.` Use for "review this PR", "review my diff", "audit this file". Skips formatting nits unless they change meaning. (Tools: Read, Grep, Bash)
- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- code-simplifier:code-simplifier: Simplifies and refines code for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. Focuses on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise. (Tools: All tools)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- caveman:caveman-commit: Generate terse caveman-style commit message

- skill-creator:skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- frontend-design:frontend-design: Guidance for distinctive, intentional visual design when building new UI or reshaping an existing one. Helps with aesthetic direction, typography, and making choices that don't read as templated defaults.
- caveman:cavecrew: Decision guide for delegating to caveman-style subagents. Tells the main thread WHEN to spawn `cavecrew-investigator` (locate code), `cavecrew-builder` (1-2 file edit), or `cavecrew-reviewer` (diff review) instead of doing the work inline or using vanilla `Explore`. Subagent output is caveman-compressed so the tool-result injected back into main context is ~60% smaller — main context lasts longer across long sessions. Trigger: "delegate to subagent", "use cavecrew", "spawn investigator/builder/reviewer", "save context", "compressed agent output".
- caveman:caveman-compress: Compress natural language memory files (CLAUDE.md, todos, preferences) into caveman format to save input tokens. Preserves all technical substance, code, URLs, and structure. Compressed version overwrites the original file. Human-readable backup saved as FILE.original.md. Trigger: /caveman-compress FILEPATH or "compress memory file"
- caveman:caveman-help: Quick-reference card for all caveman modes, skills, and commands. One-shot display, not a persistent mode. Trigger: /caveman-help, "caveman help", "what caveman commands", "how do I use caveman".
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

=====ROOT CLAUDE.md=====
# CLAUDE.md — engineering rules for this project

> This file is read by humans and by AI assistants (Claude, Cursor) alike. It is the **source
> of truth** for how we write code in this repository. Assistants: apply these rules without
> asking; if something conflicts with a user request, flag the conflict rather than quietly
> breaking a rule.

## Stack (short version)

- **Frontend:** TanStack Start (TS `strict`) + TanStack Query (server state) + Zustand (UI
  state) + Tailwind v4 + shadcn/ui.
- **Backend:** FastAPI (Python 3.12+) + Beanie 2.x on async PyMongo + Pydantic v2. Packaging:
  `uv`.
- **Database:** MongoDB (Atlas in the cloud, `mongodb-atlas-local` locally and in CI).
  Transactions require a replica set; vectors go through Atlas Vector Search.
- **Type bridge:** OpenAPI -> `@hey-api/openapi-ts` (a generated client, never hand-edited).

=====skills/api-lookup/SKILL.md=====
---
name: api-lookup
description: Answer questions about API endpoints, request or response shapes and error codes from the live schema. Use instead of grepping route files, which go stale, whenever a question is about what the API actually exposes.
---

# Ask the schema, not the files

The OpenAPI schema is generated from the running code, so it cannot drift. Route files can.

## The committed artifact

```bash
python3 -c "import json; print(*json.load(open('backend/openapi.json'))['paths'], sep='\n')"
```

## The live schema (locally, dev or test only)

```bash
curl -s "http://localhost:${API_PORT:-8000}/openapi.json" | python3 -m json.tool | head -40
```

`/docs`, `/redoc` and `/openapi.json` are **disabled outside dev/test** — in production they are
a ready-made manual for the API, complete with the error-code catalogue.

## Useful queries

```bash
# the shape of a single response
python3 -c "
import json; s = json.load(open('backend/openapi.json'))
print(json.dumps(s['components']['schemas']['CurrentUserResponse'], indent=2))"

# every error code the API can return
grep -rn 'class ApiError\|class AuthError' -A 12 backend/src/app/core/domain/errors.py
```

## The error contract

Every failure — domain, 404, 405, 422, 500, or a middleware rejection — returns the same shape:

```json
{ "code": "not_found", "message": "No such resource.", "request_id": "1bdec8c6…" }
```

`request_id` matches the `X-Request-Id` response header, so a user report maps to a log line.
Validation errors additionally carry `detail` with the field-level information.

## After changing the API

The schema and the TS client are committed, and CI fails on drift:

```bash
cd backend && uv run dump-openapi
pnpm --filter web generate:api
```
=====skills/new-migration/SKILL.md=====
---
name: new-migration
description: Change the shape of stored data, add an index or a collection validator. Use when a document gains, loses or renames a field, or when a query needs a new index.
---

# Change data safely

Mongo has no schema, which removes the migration but **not** the compatibility problem: during a
rollout two versions of the code read the same documents.

## Which case is this

| Change | What to do |
|---|---|
| A new field | Nothing — give it a default and old documents read fine. This is the freedom Mongo was chosen for. |
| A new index | Declare it in the document's `Settings.indexes`, then `uv run ensure-indexes` as a release step. |
| Moving/splitting/deriving a field | A Beanie migration in `backend/migrations/`, expand-contract. |
| Dropping a field | Only after every reader has shipped. Separate step, separate deploy. |

## Expand-contract, three deploys

1. **Expand** — add the new field with a default, write both. Old code keeps working.
2. **Backfill** — a Beanie migration in `backend/migrations/`, run once.
3. **Contract** — stop reading the old field, then drop it.

## The migration file

```python
# migrations/20260816_120000_split_user_name.py
from beanie import iterative_migration

from app.models.auth import User


class Forward:
    @iterative_migration()
    async def split_full_name(self, input_document: User, output_document: User) -> None: ...


class Backward:
    @iterative_migration()
    async def merge_names(self, input_document: User, output_document: User) -> None: ...
```

**A `Backward` class is mandatory** — `docs/conventions/04` requires reversibility and Mongo will
not enforce it for you.

```bash
uv run beanie migrate --uri "$MONGODB_URL" --database "$MONGODB_DATABASE" -p migrations
```

## Indexes and validators

Both are applied by the same deployment step, **before** traffic reaches the new instances:

```bash
uv run ensure-indexes
```

On dev the application does it at startup; on staging/prod it does not, because building an
index on a large collection eats I/O.

The `$jsonSchema` validators are generated from the models (`app/db/validation.py`) and check
presence plus BSON type of top-level fields. `additionalProperties` stays allowed on purpose:
expand-contract needs a new field to be writable before the validator that knows about it ships.

## Do not forget

- A new document goes into `app/documents.py`.
- A new field that is required with no default breaks every existing document.
- `tests/test_collection_validation.py` proves the validator accepts what the model writes — run
  it after changing a document.
=====skills/query-mongo/SKILL.md=====
---
name: query-mongo
description: Query MongoDB by hand — from mongosh, a script or an ad-hoc pymongo session — without scanning a collection. Use whenever you need to look at stored data, count documents, check what a query would return, or debug something against the database.
---

# Query Mongo without scanning it

An ad-hoc query is written once and forgotten; the collection it runs against grows for years.
Everything below exists so a debugging session cannot become the incident.

## Connect

```bash
docker compose exec -T db mongosh \
  "REDACTED" --quiet --eval '…'
```

`authSource=admin` is not optional — the user is created in `admin`, and without it the
connection fails with a bare `Authentication failed` that reads like a wrong password.

**Before touching anything shared, ask which database.** On a local container the answer is
obvious; against a staging or production cluster it never is, and the read-only assumption is
yours to confirm, not to infer from the collection name.

## Look before you query

```javascript
db.users.estimatedDocumentCount()   // O(1), reads collection metadata
db.users.getIndexes()               // what you are allowed to filter and sort on
```

**Never `countDocuments({})` to see how big a collection is.** It walks the whole collection or
index to produce an exact number nobody needed. `estimatedDocumentCount()` answers from metadata
in constant time. Use `countDocuments` only with a selective filter, and only when the exact
number matters.

## Then query

Three rules, in order of how much damage they prevent:

1. **Filter only on indexed fields.** `getIndexes()` told you which. A filter on anything else is
   a collection scan.
2. **Always `.limit()`.** You are reading to understand, not to export. Ten documents answer
   almost every question.
3. **Project what you need.** `find(filter, {email: 1, created_at: 1})` — a document can be large
   and you rarely want all of it. Never return `password_hash` or `token_hash` to a terminal.

```javascript
db.users.find({email: "someone@example.com"}, {email: 1, created_at: 1}).limit(10)
```

**Sorting needs an index too.** An unindexed sort happens in memory with a 32 MB ceiling and
fails outright above it. Identifiers here are `ObjectId`, whose leading bytes are a timestamp, so
`sort({_id: -1})` is a free "newest first" — reach for that before adding an index on
`created_at`.

**Page with `_id`, not `skip`.** `skip(n)` walks and discards `n` documents every time, so page
500 costs 500 pages of work: `find({_id: {$lt: lastSeenId}}).sort({_id: -1}).limit(20)`.

## Check the plan when it matters

```javascript
db.users.find({email: "x@y.z"}).explain("executionStats").executionStats
```

Read three numbers:

- `nReturned` — what you got.
- `totalDocsExamined` — what the server touched. Close to `nReturned` is healthy; orders of
  magnitude larger means a scan.
- `totalKeysExamined` — index entries read.

The winning stage tells you the same in one word: `IXSCAN`/`EXPRESS_IXSCAN` means an index was
used, **`COLLSCAN` means the whole collection was read**.

## Seatbelts

```bash
cd backend && uv run strict-queries      # notablescan on locally; --off to revert
```

The database then rejects an unindexed query instead of running it — the same guard the test
suite runs under. Turn it on before exploratory work; a mistake becomes an error message rather
than a stalled server.

For a one-off against something bigger, cap the query itself:

```javascript
db.users.find({…}).maxTimeMS(5000)
```

## Never

- A write without a filter. `updateMany({}, …)` and `deleteMany({})` touch every document.
- `$where` or `mapReduce` — they execute JavaScript inside the server, and a repository contract
  forbids them in application code for the same reason.
- Building a filter by pasting a value into a string. Pass it as a value; `{"_id": "<hex>"}` is
  also wrong — an identifier has to be an `ObjectId`, or the query silently matches nothing.
=====skills/run-checks/SKILL.md=====
---
name: run-checks
description: Run every quality gate the way CI does, across both toolchains. Use before committing, before opening a PR, or when the user asks whether everything passes. Also use to reproduce a CI failure locally.
---

# Run every gate

Two toolchains, four groups. Run them in this order — the cheap ones fail fastest.

## Frontend

```bash
pnpm verify        # biome ci -> tsc -> dependency-cruiser -> vitest -> vite build
```

`pnpm ci` is a **built-in pnpm command** (clean install), not our aggregate. The aggregate is
`pnpm verify`.

## Backend

```bash
cd backend
uv run ruff check src tests scripts
uv run ruff format --check src tests scripts
uv run mypy                 # strict, src + tests
uv run lint-imports         # 6 layer contracts
uv run pytest               # needs Docker: testcontainers starts Mongo and Redis
```

## End to end

```bash
cd frontend && WEB_PORT=3100 API_PORT=8100 pnpm test:e2e
```

Requires `docker compose up -d`. Playwright starts its own backend and frontend.

The backend is layer-first, so one area spans five directories plus **two registries**. Missing

| Layer | File | Contains |
|---|---|---|
| HTTP | `src/app/routes/<area>.py` | endpoints only: statuses, cookies, mapping errors |
| Contract | `src/app/schemas/<area>.py` | request/response models, `StrictRequest` for input |
| Logic | `src/app/services/<area>.py` | business rules, transaction boundaries, no HTTP |
| Queries | `src/app/repositories/<area>.py` | every database call, nothing else |
| Document | `src/app/models/<area>.py` | the Beanie document plus `Settings.indexes` |

## The two registries — both are mandatory

```python
# src/app/routes/api.py
api_router.include_router(new_router)      # without it the route 404s

# src/app/documents.py
DOCUMENT_MODELS = (..., NewDocument)       # without it: CollectionWasNotInitialized
```

Run `uv run lint-imports` — these fail loudly if the layering slips:

- a route importing `repositories`, `models` or the database client **directly**,
- a service or repository importing FastAPI, Starlette or `schemas`,

# Change data safely

Mongo has no schema, which removes the migration but **not** the compatibility problem: during a
rollout two versions of the code read the same documents.

## Which case is this

| Change | What to do |
|---|---|
| A new field | Nothing — give it a default and old documents read fine. This is the freedom Mongo was chosen for. |
| A new index | Declare it in the document's `Settings.indexes`, then `uv run ensure-indexes` as a release step. |
| Moving/splitting/deriving a field | A Beanie migration in `backend/migrations/`, expand-contract. |
| Dropping a field | Only after every reader has shipped. Separate step, separate deploy. |

## Expand-contract, three deploys

1. **Expand** — add the new field with a default, write both. Old code keeps working.
2. **Backfill** — a Beanie migration in `backend/migrations/`, run once.
3. **Contract** — stop reading the old field, then drop it.

## The migration file

```python
# migrations/20260816_120000_split_user_name.py
from beanie import iterative_migration

from app.models.auth import User


class Forward:
    @iterative_migration()
    async def split_full_name(self, input_document: User, output_document: User) -> None: ...


class Backward:
    @iterative_migration()
    async def merge_names(self, input_document: User, output_document: User) -> None: ...
```

**A `Backward` class is mandatory** — `docs/conventions/04` requires reversibility and Mongo will
not enforce it for you.

```bash
uv run beanie migrate --uri "$MONGODB_URL" --database "$MONGODB_DATABASE" -p migrations
```

## Indexes and validators

Both are applied by the same deployment step, **before** traffic reaches the new instances:

```bash
uv run ensure-indexes
```

On dev the application does it at startup; on staging/prod it does not, because building an
index on a large collection eats I/O.

The `$jsonSchema` validators are generated from the models (`app/db/validation.py`) and check
presence plus BSON type of top-level fields. `additionalProperties` stays allowed on purpose:
expand-contract needs a new field to be writable before the validator that knows about it ships.

## Do not forget

- A new document goes into `app/documents.py`.
- A new field that is required with no default breaks every existing document.
- `tests/test_collection_validation.py` proves the validator accepts what the model writes — run
  it after changing a document.

# Query Mongo without scanning it

An ad-hoc query is written once and forgotten; the collection it runs against grows for years.
Everything below exists so a debugging session cannot become the incident.

## Connect

```bash
docker compose exec -T db mongosh \
  "REDACTED" --quiet --eval '…'
```

`authSource=admin` is not optional — the user is created in `admin`, and without it the
connection fails with a bare `Authentication failed` that reads like a wrong password.

**Before touching anything shared, ask which database.** On a local container the answer is
obvious; against a staging or production cluster it never is, and the read-only assumption is
yours to confirm, not to infer from the collection name.

## Look before you query

```javascript
db.users.estimatedDocumentCount()   // O(1), reads collection metadata
db.users.getIndexes()               // what you are allowed to filter and sort on
```

**Never `countDocuments({})` to see how big a collection is.** It walks the whole collection or
index to produce an exact number nobody needed. `estimatedDocumentCount()` answers from metadata
in constant time. Use `countDocuments` only with a selective filter, and only when the exact
number matters.

## Then query

Three rules, in order of how much damage they prevent:

1. **Filter only on indexed fields.** `getIndexes()` told you which. A filter on anything else is
   a collection scan.
2. **Always `.limit()`.** You are reading to understand, not to export. Ten documents answer
   almost every question.
3. **Project what you need.** `find(filter, {email: 1, created_at: 1})` — a document can be large
   and you rarely want all of it. Never return `password_hash` or `token_hash` to a terminal.

```javascript
db.users.find({email: "someone@example.com"}, {email: 1, created_at: 1}).limit(10)
```

**Sorting needs an index too.** An unindexed sort happens in memory with a 32 MB ceiling and
fails outright above it. Identifiers here are `ObjectId`, whose leading bytes are a timestamp, so
`sort({_id: -1})` is a free "newest first" — reach for that before adding an index on
`created_at`.

**Page with `_id`, not `skip`.** `skip(n)` walks and discards `n` documents every time, so page
500 costs 500 pages of work: `find({_id: {$lt: lastSeenId}}).sort({_id: -1}).limit(20)`.

## Check the plan when it matters

```javascript
db.users.find({email: "x@y.z"}).explain("executionStats").executionStats
```

Read three numbers:

- `nReturned` — what you got.
- `totalDocsExamined` — what the server touched. Close to `nReturned` is healthy; orders of
  magnitude larger means a scan.
- `totalKeysExamined` — index entries read.

The winning stage tells you the same in one word: `IXSCAN`/`EXPRESS_IXSCAN` means an index was
used, **`COLLSCAN` means the whole collection was read**.

## Seatbelts

```bash
cd backend && uv run strict-queries      # notablescan on locally; --off to revert
```

The database then rejects an unindexed query instead of running it — the same guard the test
suite runs under. Turn it on before exploratory work; a mistake becomes an error message rather
than a stalled server.

For a one-off against something bigger, cap the query itself:

```javascript
db.users.find({…}).maxTimeMS(5000)
```

## Never

- A write without a filter. `updateMany({}, …)` and `deleteMany({})` touch every document.
- `$where` or `mapReduce` — they execute JavaScript inside the server, and a repository contract
  forbids them in application code for the same reason.
- Building a filter by pasting a value into a string. Pass it as a value; `{"_id": "<hex>"}` is
  also wrong — an identifier has to be an `ObjectId`, or the query silently matches nothing.

=====code-review.md=====
---
description: Strict maintainability review of a diff — abstraction quality, files that sprawl, conditionals grafted into unrelated flows. Use for a deep code quality review or a harsh pre-merge audit.
argument-hint: [scope, e.g. "against main" or a path]

# Code review

$ARGUMENTS — if no scope is given, review `git diff main...HEAD`.

Be **ambitious about structure**. Do not stop at local cleanups: look for the restructuring that
makes whole branches, helpers and conditionals disappear. Prefer deleting complexity over
rearranging it. The best outcome is a change that looks inevitable in hindsight.

## What to flag

1. **A file crossing ~500 lines**, or growing towards it. Extract before it sprawls; this
   codebase has none that large and that is worth keeping.
2. **Ad-hoc conditionals grafted into unrelated flows.** A new `if` in a function that did not
   care about that concern is a design problem, not a nit. Push the logic into the layer that
   owns it.
3. **Logic in the wrong layer.** A route doing business logic, a service touching
   `Request`/`Response`, a query outside `repositories/`. The import contracts catch the import,
   not the smell — you have to catch the smell.
4. **Unnecessary optionality.** `X | None` that no caller can produce, a fallback papering over
   an unclear invariant. Make the boundary explicit instead.
5. **Suppressions and casts.** `any`, `type: ignore`, `noqa` — each has to be a real false
   positive with a written reason, or it is a bug waiting.
6. **Claims without evidence.** A comment saying something is faster or safer, with no
   measurement behind it. Either measure it or drop the claim.
7. **Tests that cannot fail.** A test asserting on a mock, or one whose subject could be deleted
   while it stays green. Check the important ones by mutation: break the code, confirm red.

## What not to flag

- Formatting — Biome and Ruff own that.
- Anything a contract already enforces and that currently passes.
- Personal style preferences that the file does not already follow.

## Output

Findings ordered by severity, each with `file:line`, the concrete failure it enables, and the
smallest change that fixes it. If a restructuring would remove a whole class of the findings,
lead with that instead of listing them one by one.

# Deslop

$ARGUMENTS — if no scope is given, review the working tree plus the last commit.

Remove what a careful author of *this* codebase would not have written:

- **Comments that restate the code.** A comment here earns its place by explaining *why*, a
  measurement, or a trap. `# increment the counter` does not.
- **Defensive code that does not match the area.** A `try/except` around a call that cannot
  fail, or a null check on a value the type system already guarantees. Trusted, validated call
  paths do not need belt and braces.
- **Casts and suppressions that dodge the type system**: `as any`, `# type: ignore` without a
  justification, `@ts-expect-error`, `# noqa` on something that should simply be fixed. This
  repository has exactly one suppression, and it carries a paragraph explaining why.
- **Style inconsistent with the file.** Match the surrounding density of comments, naming and
  idiom rather than importing a different house style.
- **Dead code and commented-out blocks.** Git remembers them.

Do not remove:

- comments recording a measurement, a defect or a deliberate trade-off — those are the ones
  worth keeping,
- tests that look redundant but are negative or positive controls.

Afterwards run the gates (`/run-checks` or the skill of that name) and report in one to three
sentences what you removed.

# Fix merge conflicts

Work from the repository root. If this is not a git repository, stop and say so.

Do not ask questions — pick sensible defaults and explain them in the summary. Do not push and
do not tag; commit locally only.

## Plan

1. Find the conflicts: `git status --porcelain` plus a search for conflict markers.
2. Resolve per file, preserving both sides' intent where they are compatible. Where they are
   mutually exclusive, keep the variant that type-checks and preserves the existing public API.

description: Strict maintainability review of a diff — abstraction quality, files that sprawl, conditionals grafted into unrelated flows. Use for a deep code quality review or a harsh pre-merge audit.
argument-hint: [scope, e.g. "against main" or a path]

# Code review

$ARGUMENTS — if no scope is given, review `git diff main...HEAD`.

Be **ambitious about structure**. Do not stop at local cleanups: look for the restructuring that
makes whole branches, helpers and conditionals disappear. Prefer deleting complexity over
rearranging it. The best outcome is a change that looks inevitable in hindsight.

## What to flag

1. **A file crossing ~500 lines**, or growing towards it. Extract before it sprawls; this
   codebase has none that large and that is worth keeping.
2. **Ad-hoc conditionals grafted into unrelated flows.** A new `if` in a function that did not
   care about that concern is a design problem, not a nit. Push the logic into the layer that
   owns it.
3. **Logic in the wrong layer.** A route doing business logic, a service touching
   `Request`/`Response`, a query outside `repositories/`. The import contracts catch the import,
   not the smell — you have to catch the smell.
4. **Unnecessary optionality.** `X | None` that no caller can produce, a fallback papering over
   an unclear invariant. Make the boundary explicit instead.
5. **Suppressions and casts.** `any`, `type: ignore`, `noqa` — each has to be a real false
   positive with a written reason, or it is a bug waiting.
6. **Claims without evidence.** A comment saying something is faster or safer, with no
   measurement behind it. Either measure it or drop the claim.
7. **Tests that cannot fail.** A test asserting on a mock, or one whose subject could be deleted
   while it stays green. Check the important ones by mutation: break the code, confirm red.

## What not to flag

- Formatting — Biome and Ruff own that.
- Anything a contract already enforces and that currently passes.
- Personal style preferences that the file does not already follow.

## Output

Findings ordered by severity, each with `file:line`, the concrete failure it enables, and the
smallest change that fixes it. If a restructuring would remove a whole class of the findings,
lead with that instead of listing them one by one.

# Deslop

$ARGUMENTS — if no scope is given, review the working tree plus the last commit.

Remove what a careful author of *this* codebase would not have written:

- **Comments that restate the code.** A comment here earns its place by explaining *why*, a
  measurement, or a trap. `# increment the counter` does not.
- **Defensive code that does not match the area.** A `try/except` around a call that cannot
  fail, or a null check on a value the type system already guarantees. Trusted, validated call
  paths do not need belt and braces.
- **Casts and suppressions that dodge the type system**: `as any`, `# type: ignore` without a
  justification, `@ts-expect-error`, `# noqa` on something that should simply be fixed. This
  repository has exactly one suppression, and it carries a paragraph explaining why.
- **Style inconsistent with the file.** Match the surrounding density of comments, naming and
  idiom rather than importing a different house style.
- **Dead code and commented-out blocks.** Git remembers them.

Do not remove:

- comments recording a measurement, a defect or a deliberate trade-off — those are the ones
  worth keeping,
- tests that look redundant but are negative or positive controls.

Afterwards run the gates (`/run-checks` or the skill of that name) and report in one to three
sentences what you removed.

/** Frontend module boundaries — see docs/conventions/05-architecture-enforcement.md */
module.exports = {
  forbidden: [
    {
      name: "no-circular",
      severity: "error",
      comment: "Cycles between modules are forbidden.",
      from: {},
      to: { circular: true },
    },
    {
      name: "feature-isolation",
      severity: "error",
      comment: "features/* import each other only through the public index.ts.",
      from: { path: "^src/features/([^/]+)/" },
      to: { path: "^src/features/(?!$1)[^/]+/(?!index\\.ts$)" },
    },
    {
      name: "ui-kit-knows-nothing-about-features",
      severity: "error",
      comment:
        "components/ui holds stateless design primitives. Importing a feature from there " +
        "means the component is in the wrong directory — it belongs in features/<name>/.",
      from: { path: "^src/components/" },
      to: { path: "^src/(features|routes)/" },
    },
    {
      name: "generated-api-client-is-private",
      severity: "error",
      comment:
        "The OpenAPI client is generated — consume it via src/lib/api/index.ts, not file by file.",
      from: { pathNot: "^src/lib/api/" },
      to: { path: "^src/lib/api/(?!index\\.ts$)" },
    },
  ],
  options: {
    doNotFollow: { path: "node_modules" },
    exclude: { path: "routeTree\\.gen\\.ts$" },
    tsConfig: { fileName: "tsconfig.json" },
  },
};
=====pre-commit=====
# CI parity, locally. Install with: uvx pre-commit install
# Run across the repo: uvx pre-commit run --all-files
# Without this, a plain `pre-commit install` wires up only the `pre-commit` hook and the
# commit-message hook would never run.
default_install_hook_types: [pre-commit, commit-msg]

repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/pre-commit/pre-commit-hooks
    rev: v6.0.0
    hooks:
      - id: check-merge-conflict
      - id: end-of-file-fixer
      - id: trailing-whitespace
      - id: check-yaml
      - id: check-toml
      - id: detect-private-key

  - repo: https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks
    rev: v8.30.0
    hooks:
      - id: gitleaks

  # The doctor script is plain bash (it has to work when nothing is installed yet), so it gets
  # its own linter too — "everything is linted" has no exceptions.
  - repo: https://github.com/koalaman/shellcheck-precommit
    rev: v0.11.0
    hooks:
      - id: shellcheck

  - repo: https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff-pre-commit
    rev: v0.16.1
    hooks:
      - id: ruff-check
        args: [--fix]
        files: ^backend/
      - id: ruff-format
        files: ^backend/

  - repo: https://github.com/biomejs/pre-commit
    rev: v2.5.6
    hooks:
      - id: biome-check
        additional_dependencies: ["@biomejs/biome@2.5.6"]

  - repo: local
    hooks:
      - id: mypy
        name: mypy (backend, strict)
        entry: uv run --directory backend mypy
        language: system
        pass_filenames: false
        files: ^backend/.*\.py$
      - id: lint-imports
        name: import-linter (layer boundaries)
        entry: uv run --directory backend lint-imports
        language: system
        pass_filenames: false
        files: ^backend/.*\.py$
      - id: commit-message-format
        name: commit message format (docs/conventions/04)
        entry: scripts/check-commit-message.sh
        language: script
        # The only commit-msg hook — it receives the path to the message file, not a list of
        # changed files. Requires: pre-commit install --hook-type commit-msg
        stages: [commit-msg]

name: CI

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  frontend:
    name: Frontend (TS)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@0ebf47130e4866e96fce0953f49152a61190b271 # v6.0.9
      - uses: actions/setup-node@820762786026740c76f36085b0efc47a31fe5020 # v7.0.0
        with:
          node-version-file: .nvmrc
          cache: pnpm
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: pnpm lint # biome ci: lint + format + import order (whole repo)
      - run: pnpm typecheck
      - run: pnpm boundaries # dependency-cruiser (module boundaries)
      - run: pnpm test # vitest + Testing Library + MSW
      - run: pnpm build
      - name: routeTree.gen.ts matches routes/
        run: git diff --exit-code -- frontend/src/routeTree.gen.ts
      - name: OpenAPI client matches the schema
        run: |
          pnpm --filter web generate:api
          git diff --exit-code -- frontend/src/lib/api/generated

  backend:
    name: Backend (Python)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: backend
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@c771a70e6277c0a99b617c7a806ffedaca235ff9 # v9.0.0
        with:
          enable-cache: true
          python-version: "3.12"
          working-directory: backend
      - run: uv sync --frozen
      - run: uv run ruff check src tests scripts
      - run: uv run ruff format --check src tests scripts
      - run: uv run mypy
      - run: uv run lint-imports # import-linter (layer boundaries)
      # testcontainers starts mongodb-atlas-local (a single-node replica set — required for
      # transactions) plus redis for the shared rate-limit counter tests. The Mongo image weighs
      # ~650 MB, so the first pull in a job takes tens of seconds.
      - run: uv run pytest
      - name: openapi.json matches the routers
        run: |
          uv run dump-openapi
          git diff --exit-code -- openapi.json

  security:
    name: Dependency security
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@0ebf47130e4866e96fce0953f49152a61190b271 # v6.0.9
      - uses: actions/setup-node@820762786026740c76f36085b0efc47a31fe5020 # v7.0.0
        with:
          node-version-file: .nvmrc
          cache: pnpm
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@c771a70e6277c0a99b617c7a806ffedaca235ff9 # v9.0.0
        with:
          enable-cache: true
          python-version: "3.12"
          working-directory: backend
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      # A separate job, because this is the only gate that depends on an EXTERNAL advisory
      # database: it can turn red without a single change in the repo. Splitting it out keeps
      # "you broke the code" distinguishable from "a new vulnerability was published".
      - name: JS dependency vulnerabilities
        run: pnpm audit --audit-level=high
      - run: uv sync --frozen
        working-directory: backend
      - name: Python dependency vulnerabilities
        # `--skip-editable` skips the application package itself (no advisory covers it).
        run: uv run --with pip-audit pip-audit --skip-editable
        working-directory: backend

  e2e:
    name: E2E (Playwright)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      db:
        # Ten sam obraz co docker-compose i testy: replica set (transakcje) + Atlas Search.
        image: mongodb/mongodb-atlas-local:8.2
        env:
          MONGODB_INITDB_ROOT_USERNAME: app
          MONGODB_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD: app
        ports: ["27018:27017"]
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "mongosh -u app -p app --quiet --eval 'db.adminCommand({ping:1}).ok'"
          --health-interval 10s
          --health-timeout 5s
          --health-retries 30
      redis:
        # The same shared rate-limit counter as locally and in production — without it CI would
        # exercise a different code path (process memory) than the target environments.
        image: redis:8-alpine
        ports: ["6380:6379"]
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "redis-cli ping"
          --health-interval 5s
          --health-timeout 3s
          --health-retries 10
    env:
      MONGODB_URL: REDACTED
      MONGODB_DATABASE: app
      RATE_LIMIT_STORAGE_URL: redis://localhost:6380
      AUTH_SECRET: ci-secret-not-used-anywhere-else
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@0ebf47130e4866e96fce0953f49152a61190b271 # v6.0.9
      - uses: actions/setup-node@820762786026740c76f36085b0efc47a31fe5020 # v7.0.0

          node-version-file: .nvmrc
          cache: pnpm
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@c771a70e6277c0a99b617c7a806ffedaca235ff9 # v9.0.0
        with:
          enable-cache: true
          python-version: "3.12"
          working-directory: backend
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: uv sync --frozen
        working-directory: backend
      - run: pnpm --filter web exec playwright install --with-deps chromium
      # Playwright sam podnosi backend i front — patrz playwright.config.ts.
      # Indexes are created at application startup (APP_ENV=dev), so there is no separate
      # migration step.
      - run: pnpm --filter web test:e2e
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@043fb46d1a93c77aae656e7c1c64a875d1fc6a0a # v7.0.1
        if: failure()
        with:
          name: playwright-report
          path: frontend/playwright-report/
          retention-days: 7

module.exports = {
  forbidden: [
    {
      name: "no-circular",
      severity: "error",
      comment: "Cycles between modules are forbidden.",
      from: {},
      to: { circular: true },

      name: "feature-isolation",
      severity: "error",
      comment: "features/* import each other only through the public index.ts.",
      from: { path: "^src/features/([^/]+)/" },
      to: { path: "^src/features/(?!$1)[^/]+/(?!index\\.ts$)" },

      comment:

      from: { path: "^src/components/" },
      to: { path: "^src/(features|routes)/" },

# CI parity, locally. Install with: uvx pre-commit install
# Run across the repo: uvx pre-commit run --all-files
# Without this, a plain `pre-commit install` wires up only the `pre-commit` hook and the
# commit-message hook would never run.
default_install_hook_types: [pre-commit, commit-msg]

repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/pre-commit/pre-commit-hooks
    rev: v6.0.0
    hooks:
      - id: check-merge-conflict
      - id: end-of-file-fixer
      - id: trailing-whitespace
      - id: check-yaml
      - id: check-toml
      - id: detect-private-key

  - repo: https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks
    rev: v8.30.0
    hooks:
      - id: gitleaks

  # The doctor script is plain bash (it has to work when nothing is installed yet), so it gets
  # its own linter too — "everything is linted" has no exceptions.
  - repo: https://github.com/koalaman/shellcheck-precommit
    rev: v0.11.0
    hooks:
      - id: shellcheck

  - repo: https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff-pre-commit
    rev: v0.16.1
    hooks:
      - id: ruff-check
        args: [--fix]
        files: ^backend/
      - id: ruff-format
        files: ^backend/

  - repo: https://github.com/biomejs/pre-commit
    rev: v2.5.6
    hooks:
      - id: biome-check
        additional_dependencies: ["@biomejs/biome@2.5.6"]

  - repo: local
    hooks:
      - id: mypy
        name: mypy (backend, strict)
        entry: uv run --directory backend mypy
        language: system
        pass_filenames: false
        files: ^backend/.*\.py$
      - id: lint-imports
        name: import-linter (layer boundaries)
        entry: uv run --directory backend lint-imports
        language: system
        pass_filenames: false
        files: ^backend/.*\.py$
      - id: commit-message-format
        name: commit message format (docs/conventions/04)
        entry: scripts/check-commit-message.sh
        language: script
        # The only commit-msg hook — it receives the path to the message file, not a list of
        # changed files. Requires: pre-commit install --hook-type commit-msg
        stages: [commit-msg]

name: CI

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  frontend:
    name: Frontend (TS)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@0ebf47130e4866e96fce0953f49152a61190b271 # v6.0.9
      - uses: actions/setup-node@820762786026740c76f36085b0efc47a31fe5020 # v7.0.0
        with:
          node-version-file: .nvmrc
          cache: pnpm
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: pnpm lint # biome ci: lint + format + import order (whole repo)
      - run: pnpm typecheck
      - run: pnpm boundaries # dependency-cruiser (module boundaries)
      - run: pnpm test # vitest + Testing Library + MSW
      - run: pnpm build
      - name: routeTree.gen.ts matches routes/
        run: git diff --exit-code -- frontend/src/routeTree.gen.ts
      - name: OpenAPI client matches the schema
        run: |
          pnpm --filter web generate:api
          git diff --exit-code -- frontend/src/lib/api/generated

  backend:
    name: Backend (Python)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: backend
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@c771a70e6277c0a99b617c7a806ffedaca235ff9 # v9.0.0
        with:
          enable-cache: true
          python-version: "3.12"
          working-directory: backend
      - run: uv sync --frozen
      - run: uv run ruff check src tests scripts
      - run: uv run ruff format --check src tests scripts
      - run: uv run mypy
      - run: uv run lint-imports # import-linter (layer boundaries)
      # testcontainers starts mongodb-atlas-local (a single-node replica set — required for
      # transactions) plus redis for the shared rate-limit counter tests. The Mongo image weighs
      # ~650 MB, so the first pull in a job takes tens of seconds.
      - run: uv run pytest
      - name: openapi.json matches the routers
        run: |
          uv run dump-openapi
          git diff --exit-code -- openapi.json

  security:
    name: Dependency security
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@0ebf47130e4866e96fce0953f49152a61190b271 # v6.0.9
      - uses: actions/setup-node@820762786026740c76f36085b0efc47a31fe5020 # v7.0.0
        with:
          node-version-file: .nvmrc
          cache: pnpm
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@c771a70e6277c0a99b617c7a806ffedaca235ff9 # v9.0.0
        with:
          enable-cache: true
          python-version: "3.12"
          working-directory: backend
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      # A separate job, because this is the only gate that depends on an EXTERNAL advisory
      # database: it can turn red without a single change in the repo. Splitting it out keeps
      # "you broke the code" distinguishable from "a new vulnerability was published".
      - name: JS dependency vulnerabilities
        run: pnpm audit --audit-level=high
      - run: uv sync --frozen
        working-directory: backend
      - name: Python dependency vulnerabilities
        # `--skip-editable` skips the application package itself (no advisory covers it).
        run: uv run --with pip-audit pip-audit --skip-editable
        working-directory: backend

    name: E2E (Playwright)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

      - run: pnpm --filter web test:e2e

=====doctor.sh=====
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Checks the environment BEFORE the first run: tool versions, pin consistency and free ports.
#
# It grew out of concrete failures, not predictions:
#   - a locally installed mongod stole the port from Docker and the application quietly talked
#     to a different database,
#   - Node 23 passed most gates, but dependency-cruiser supports only ^22||^24,
#   - a zombie server on :3000 was "borrowed" by Playwright instead of starting its own.
#
# Deliberately plain bash: it has to work when NOTHING is installed yet.
set -uo pipefail

cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." || exit 1

RED=$'\033[31m'; YELLOW=$'\033[33m'; GREEN=$'\033[32m'; DIM=$'\033[2m'; OFF=$'\033[0m'
errors=0
warnings=0

ok()   { printf '  %sOK%s   %s\n' "$GREEN" "$OFF" "$1"; }
warn() { printf '  %sWARN%s %s\n' "$YELLOW" "$OFF" "$1"; warnings=$((warnings + 1)); }
bad()  { printf '  %sFAIL%s %s\n' "$RED" "$OFF" "$1"; errors=$((errors + 1)); }

# --- pins: mise.toml has to agree with .nvmrc, which CI uses ---
printf '\n%sPin consistency%s\n' "$DIM" "$OFF"
nvmrc_node="$(tr -d '[:space:]' < .nvmrc 2>/dev/null)"
mise_node="$(grep -E '^node[[:space:]]*=' mise.toml 2>/dev/null | sed -E 's/.*"([^"]+)".*/\1/')"
if [ -z "$nvmrc_node" ] || [ -z "$mise_node" ]; then
  warn "cannot read the Node version from .nvmrc or mise.toml"
elif [ "$nvmrc_node" = "$mise_node" ]; then
  ok "Node pinned consistently in .nvmrc and mise.toml ($nvmrc_node)"
else
  bad ".nvmrc says $nvmrc_node, mise.toml says $mise_node — CI uses .nvmrc"
fi

# --- tool versions ---
printf '\n%sTools%s\n' "$DIM" "$OFF"
check_major() { # name, version-output, required-major
  local name="$1" got="$2" want="$3"
  if [ -z "$got" ]; then bad "$name: not found (requires $want)"; return; fi
  if [ "${got%%.*}" = "$want" ]; then ok "$name $got"
  else bad "$name $got — requires $want.x"; fi
}

check_major "node" "$(node --version 2>/dev/null | tr -d 'v')" "$nvmrc_node"
check_major "pnpm" "$(pnpm --version 2>/dev/null)" "11"
python_version="$(python3 --version 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $2}')"
case "$python_version" in
  3.12.*) ok "python $python_version" ;;
  "")     bad "python3: not found (requires 3.12.x)" ;;
  *)      warn "python $python_version — CI and mise pin 3.12.x" ;;
esac
uv_version="$(uv --version 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $2}')"
if [ -n "$uv_version" ]; then
  ok "uv $uv_version"
else
  bad "uv: not found"
fi

if docker info >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  ok "docker is running"
else
  bad "docker is not responding — the database and Redis will not start, nor testcontainers"
fi

# --- porty ---
# Mongo on 27018 and Redis on 6380 (not the defaults) precisely because locally installed
# instances win over the Docker ports.
printf '\n%sPorty%s\n' "$DIM" "$OFF"
check_port() { # port, do czego, czy-nasz-kontener-go-zajmuje-to-ok
  local port="$1" what="$2"
  local pid
  pid="$(lsof -tiTCP:"$port" -sTCP:LISTEN 2>/dev/null | head -1)"
  if [ -z "$pid" ]; then
    ok "$port wolny ($what)"
    return
  fi
  local owner
  owner="$(ps -o comm= -p "$pid" 2>/dev/null | xargs basename 2>/dev/null)"
  warn "$port taken by '$owner' (pid $pid) — $what"
}

# The frontend and API ports are configurable (WEB_PORT/API_PORT) — we check the ones that
# will actually be used, so the warning is not about somebody else's process.
check_port "${WEB_PORT:-3000}" "frontend dev; a taken port gets 'borrowed' by Playwright (workaround: WEB_PORT=3100)"
check_port "${API_PORT:-8000}" "backend uvicorn (workaround: API_PORT=8100)"
check_port 27018 "MongoDB from docker-compose"
check_port 6380 "Redis from docker-compose"

# --- configuration ---
printf '\n%sConfiguration%s\n' "$DIM" "$OFF"
if [ -f .env ]; then
  if grep -q 'change-me' .env 2>/dev/null; then
    warn ".env still has AUTH_SECRET=change-me — generate one: openssl rand -hex 32"
  else
    ok ".env present"
  fi
else
  warn "no .env — copy it: cp .env.example .env (without it the defaults apply)"
fi

printf '\n'
if [ "$errors" -gt 0 ]; then
  printf '%sErrors: %d, warnings: %d%s\n' "$RED" "$errors" "$warnings" "$OFF"
  exit 1
fi
printf '%sEnvironment ready%s (warnings: %d)\n' "$GREEN" "$OFF" "$warnings"

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Enforces the commit format from docs/conventions/04: Conventional Commits.
#
# The scope is OPTIONAL and names an area of the code (`auth`, `ci`, `db`) — not a ticket number.
# A project that requires a ticket ID tightens the regex here; the skeleton assumes no tracker.
#
# Deliberately a script rather than commitlint: this is one regex, and commitlint would add
# node_modules to a path a backend developer may not even have installed.
set -euo pipefail

message_file="${1:?path to the commit message file}"
# The first non-empty, non-comment line — git appends its own '#' instructions below.
subject="$(grep -v '^#' "$message_file" | grep -v '^[[:space:]]*$' | head -n 1 || true)"

# Uppercase in the scope is allowed: a project that adds a tracker (`feat(TEA-1234): ...`)
# has no reason to fight the hook. The type itself must come from the list.
pattern='^(feat|fix|chore|hotfix|refactor|test|docs|revert)(\([A-Za-z0-9._-]+\))?!?: .+'

# Merge and revert messages generated by git have their own, non-negotiable format.
if [[ "$subject" =~ ^(Merge|Revert)\  ]]; then
  exit 0
fi

if [[ ! "$subject" =~ $pattern ]]; then
  cat >&2 <<MSG
Commit message does not match the format from docs/conventions/04.

  Got:      ${subject}
  Pattern:  type: description   or   type(scope): description
  Types:    feat, fix, chore, hotfix, refactor, test, docs, revert
  Examples: feat(auth): add passkey registration
            fix: do not echo the password in the 422 response
MSG
  exit 1
fi
=====conv08=====
# Operational skills and commands (a library)

The biggest gem from the Asystent-AI codebase: **repeatable workflows written down as
skills/commands** inside the repository, versioned with the code. An AI assistant runs them
instead of improvising, and the team gets one way of doing the usual tasks.

## How we organize them

- **Skills** in `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` (a description plus instructions and optional
  scripts/`references/`). The frontmatter `description` decides when the skill activates —
  write it concretely (triggers, "use when…", "do NOT use for…").
- **Commands** (slash) in `.claude/commands/<name>.md` — shorter, imperative procedures.
- Skills are **narrow and single-purpose**; if a description contains a lot of "either/or",
  split it into separate ones.

## What this repository actually ships

Five skills in `.claude/skills/`, each written because we hit the trap it describes rather than
because a list said so:

| Skill | Why it exists |
|---|---|
| `run-dev` | The port dance (27018/6380, and 3000/8000 often taken), plus the fact that a visible element does not prove hydration. |
| `run-checks` | Gates spread across two toolchains, `pnpm ci` is not our aggregate, and pre-commit silently checks only files git knows about. |
| `scaffold-endpoint` | Layer-first means one area spans five directories **and two registries**; missing a registry fails at runtime, not at import. |
| `new-migration` | No schema does not remove the compatibility problem; a `Backward` class is mandatory and indexes are a release step. |
| `api-lookup` | Route files go stale, the generated schema cannot. |
| `query-mongo` | An ad-hoc query is written once and runs against a collection that grows for years: `countDocuments({})` scans, an unindexed sort dies at 32 MB, `skip(n)` walks n documents. |

Five commands in `.claude/commands/`, adapted from the Asystent-AI repository — the generic
ones, with the product-specific detail replaced by ours:

| Command | Why it exists |
|---|---|
| `/research` | Documents how an area works today, with `file:line`. Explicitly forbidden from suggesting changes — a documentarian, not a reviewer. |
| `/deslop` | Removes AI slop: comments restating code, defensive branches unusual for the area, casts and suppressions that dodge the type system. |
| `/code-review` | A strict maintainability audit that pushes for deleting complexity rather than rearranging it. Model invocation disabled: you ask for it deliberately. |
| `/post-mortem` | The template exists before the incident, which is the only time it can be written calmly. |
| `/fix-merge-conflicts` | Encodes which files must never be hand-merged (lockfiles, `openapi.json`, the generated client, `routeTree.gen.ts`) — regenerate instead. |

What we deliberately did **not** copy from that repository: 28 product-specific skills (tender
sources, legal rules, Elasticsearch sync) with no meaning here, its `mongo` skill (its access
runs through AWS SSO against their clusters) and `apply-design-engineering` (481 lines of
somebody else's course material — worth reading at the source, not vendoring).

The rest of this document is the wider catalogue worth building once the product has the
consumers for it.

## Starter set worth adding as the product grows

**Dev / quality:**

- `run-dev` — starts the backend (uvicorn) and the frontend (dev) on the agreed ports.
- `research` — documents existing code (the current state only, no change proposals).
- `deslop` — removes "AI slop": redundant comments, defensive try/except that is unusual for
  the area, `as any`/casts that work around the types.
- `fix-merge-conflicts` — resolves conflicts non-interactively and brings the repo back to
  build + test.
- `post-mortem` — produces an incident post-mortem document (timeline, root cause, impact,
  remediation).

**Scaffolding (per our layers):**

- `scaffold-endpoint` — a new area in the layer-first structure: a file in `routes/` (plus an
  entry in `routes/api.py`), `schemas/`, `services/`, `repositories/`, `models/` (plus an entry
  in `app/documents.py`) and a test. In a layer-first layout one area spans five directories, so
  scaffolding matters more here than under feature folders — by hand it is easy to forget the
  document registry or the `include_router` line.
- `scaffold-scheduled-report` — a recurring per-org report on a cron (if the product needs one).

**Ops / production:**

- `error-triage` — clusters errors from logs (Loki) -> a ticket (Linear) with a hypothesis and
  an owner (git blame) -> a digest on Slack.
- `assign-error-tickets` — assigns `error` tickets to the author of the code (git blame -> alias
  map -> Linear).
- `weekly-work-summary` — the Friday #shipping post: the week's plan versus merged PRs, ready to
  paste.

**Frontend review:**

- `apply-design-engineering` — design-engineering philosophy for UI polish (motion,
  micro-interactions, hover/active states).
- `web-design-guidelines` — a UI audit for accessibility and interface guidelines.
- `vercel-react-best-practices` — React/Next performance patterns during review.

**API:**

- `api-docs-lookup` — ask the live OpenAPI schema (`/openapi.json`) about endpoints and schemas
  instead of grepping route files.

## The "a skill instead of memory" rule

If you are doing something for the **second time** and it has repeatable steps or foot-guns,
write it down as a skill rather than keeping it in your head. Skills are the team's operational
memory; they grow with the product and are the best place for hard-won traps (e.g. "migrations
go through Neon's direct URL", "two clusters for test/prod").

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Enforces the commit format from docs/conventions/04: Conventional Commits.
#
# The scope is OPTIONAL and names an area of the code (`auth`, `ci`, `db`) — not a ticket number.
# A project that requires a ticket ID tightens the regex here; the skeleton assumes no tracker.
#
# Deliberately a script rather than commitlint: this is one regex, and commitlint would add
# node_modules to a path a backend developer may not even have installed.
set -euo pipefail

message_file="${1:?path to the commit message file}"
# The first non-empty, non-comment line — git appends its own '#' instructions below.
subject="$(grep -v '^#' "$message_file" | grep -v '^[[:space:]]*$' | head -n 1 || true)"

# Uppercase in the scope is allowed: a project that adds a tracker (`feat(TEA-1234): ...`)
# has no reason to fight the hook. The type itself must come from the list.
pattern='^(feat|fix|chore|hotfix|refactor|test|docs|revert)(\([A-Za-z0-9._-]+\))?!?: .+'

# Merge and revert messages generated by git have their own, non-negotiable format.
if [[ "$subject" =~ ^(Merge|Revert)\  ]]; then
  exit 0
fi

if [[ ! "$subject" =~ $pattern ]]; then
  cat >&2 <<MSG
Commit message does not match the format from docs/conventions/04.

  Got:      ${subject}
  Pattern:  type: description   or   type(scope): description
  Types:    feat, fix, chore, hotfix, refactor, test, docs, revert
  Examples: feat(auth): add passkey registration
            fix: do not echo the password in the 422 response
MSG
  exit 1
fi

# Operational skills and commands (a library)

The biggest gem from the Asystent-AI codebase: **repeatable workflows written down as
skills/commands** inside the repository, versioned with the code. An AI assistant runs them
instead of improvising, and the team gets one way of doing the usual tasks.

## How we organize them

- **Skills** in `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` (a description plus instructions and optional
  scripts/`references/`). The frontmatter `description` decides when the skill activates —
  write it concretely (triggers, "use when…", "do NOT use for…").
- **Commands** (slash) in `.claude/commands/<name>.md` — shorter, imperative procedures.
- Skills are **narrow and single-purpose**; if a description contains a lot of "either/or",
  split it into separate ones.

## What this repository actually ships

Five skills in `.claude/skills/`, each written because we hit the trap it describes rather than
because a list said so:

| Skill | Why it exists |
|---|---|
| `run-dev` | The port dance (27018/6380, and 3000/8000 often taken), plus the fact that a visible element does not prove hydration. |
| `run-checks` | Gates spread across two toolchains, `pnpm ci` is not our aggregate, and pre-commit silently checks only files git knows about. |
| `scaffold-endpoint` | Layer-first means one area spans five directories **and two registries**; missing a registry fails at runtime, not at import. |
| `new-migration` | No schema does not remove the compatibility problem; a `Backward` class is mandatory and indexes are a release step. |
| `api-lookup` | Route files go stale, the generated schema cannot. |
| `query-mongo` | An ad-hoc query is written once and runs against a collection that grows for years: `countDocuments({})` scans, an unindexed sort dies at 32 MB, `skip(n)` walks n documents. |

Five commands in `.claude/commands/`, adapted from the Asystent-AI repository — the generic
ones, with the product-specific detail replaced by ours:

| Command | Why it exists |
|---|---|
| `/research` | Documents how an area works today, with `file:line`. Explicitly forbidden from suggesting changes — a documentarian, not a reviewer. |
| `/deslop` | Removes AI slop: comments restating code, defensive branches unusual for the area, casts and suppressions that dodge the type system. |
| `/code-review` | A strict maintainability audit that pushes for deleting complexity rather than rearranging it. Model invocation disabled: you ask for it deliberately. |
| `/post-mortem` | The template exists before the incident, which is the only time it can be written calmly. |
| `/fix-merge-conflicts` | Encodes which files must never be hand-merged (lockfiles, `openapi.json`, the generated client, `routeTree.gen.ts`) — regenerate instead. |

What we deliberately did **not** copy from that repository: 28 product-specific skills (tender
sources, legal rules, Elasticsearch sync) with no meaning here, its `mongo` skill (its access
runs through AWS SSO against their clusters) and `apply-design-engineering` (481 lines of
somebody else's course material — worth reading at the source, not vendoring).

The rest of this document is the wider catalogue worth building once the product has the
consumers for it.

## Starter set worth adding as the product grows

**Dev / quality:**

- `run-dev` — starts the backend (uvicorn) and the frontend (dev) on the agreed ports.
- `research` — documents existing code (the current state only, no change proposals).
- `deslop` — removes "AI slop": redundant comments, defensive try/except that is unusual for
  the area, `as any`/casts that work around the types.
- `fix-merge-conflicts` — resolves conflicts non-interactively and brings the repo back to
  build + test.
- `post-mortem` — produces an incident post-mortem document (timeline, root cause, impact,
  remediation).

**Scaffolding (per our layers):**

- `scaffold-endpoint` — a new area in the layer-first structure: a file in `routes/` (plus an
  entry in `routes/api.py`), `schemas/`, `services/`, `repositories/`, `models/` (plus an entry
  in `app/documents.py`) and a test. In a layer-first layout one area spans five directories, so
  scaffolding matters more here than under feature folders — by hand it is easy to forget the
  document registry or the `include_router` line.
- `scaffold-scheduled-report` — a recurring per-org report on a cron (if the product needs one).

**Ops / production:**

- `error-triage` — clusters errors from logs (Loki) -> a ticket (Linear) with a hypothesis and
  an owner (git blame) -> a digest on Slack.
- `assign-error-tickets` — assigns `error` tickets to the author of the code (git blame -> alias
  map -> Linear).
- `weekly-work-summary` — the Friday #shipping post: the week's plan versus merged PRs, ready to
  paste.

**Frontend review:**

- `apply-design-engineering` — design-engineering philosophy for UI polish (motion,
  micro-interactions, hover/active states).
- `web-design-guidelines` — a UI audit for accessibility and interface guidelines.
- `vercel-react-best-practices` — React/Next performance patterns during review.

**API:**

- `api-docs-lookup` — ask the live OpenAPI schema (`/openapi.json`) about endpoints and schemas
  instead of grepping route files.

## The "a skill instead of memory" rule

If you are doing something for the **second time** and it has repeatable steps or foot-guns,
write it down as a skill rather than keeping it in your head. Skills are the team's operational
memory; they grow with the product and are the best place for hard-won traps (e.g. "migrations
go through Neon's direct URL", "two clusters for test/prod").

# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## Project Overview

QGIS MCP connects QGIS to Claude AI through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), enabling Claude to directly control QGIS via socket-based communication. Includes a multi-client installer (`install.py`) for easy setup.

## Architecture

The system has two components that communicate over a TCP socket (default `localhost:9876`, configurable via env vars):

1. **QGIS Plugin** (`qgis_mcp_plugin/`) - Runs inside QGIS (3.28–4.x). `server.py`'s `QgisMCPServer` creates a non-blocking TCP socket server using a `QTimer` (25ms poll interval) to accept connections and process JSON commands within QGIS's event loop; it owns the socket, framing, the auth gate and dispatch, and nothing else. The commands themselves are mixins under `handlers/` (one module per domain: `system`, `project`, `layers`, `features`, `style`, `canvas`, `processing`, `layout`, `connections`, plus `base` for the shared layer lookups), combined onto `QgisMCPServer`. `plugin.py` holds only `QgisMCPPlugin` and `classFactory` (the QGIS entry point, toolbar and menu); `configurator.py` holds the MCP-client configuration dialog. Supporting modules, all stdlib-only and `qgis`-free: `wire.py` (framing), `errors.py` (`CommandError` and friends), `registry.py` (the `@command` decorator), `constants.py` (defaults, settings prefix, `PLUGIN_DIR`). `compat.py` provides enum compatibility between QGIS 3.x and 4.x (see below).

   **Adding a command:** write the method on the mixin for its domain, decorate it with `@command` from `registry`, and add the matching `@mcp.tool` in `src/qgis_mcp/server.py`. There is no dispatch table to update - `@command` registers the name and `_dispatch` resolves it. `tests/test_plugin_structure.py` enforces both directions of that parity, plus the rule that `handlers/` modules import package-root modules with `..` and never import each other.

2. **MCP Server** (`src/qgis_mcp/server.py`) - Runs outside QGIS as a standalone Python process. Uses `FastMCP` from the `mcp` library to expose QGIS operations as MCP tools, resources, and prompts. A `_send()` helper unwraps the response envelope and raises on errors. All 118 tools are `async` with `title=` for human-readable names. Uses `ToolAnnotations` for read-only/destructive/idempotent hints. Long-running tools use `ctx.info()` for MCP logging. Destructive tools call `_confirm_destructive`, which only elicits when asked to (see `QGIS_MCP_AUTO_CONFIRM` below). An optional compound tool mode (`src/qgis_mcp/compound_tools.py`) groups tools into 27 compound tools for reduced schema overhead.

**Data flow:** Claude → MCP Server (FastMCP) → TCP socket → QGIS Plugin (QTimer loop) → PyQGIS API → response back through socket.

There is also a standalone socket client at `src/qgis_mcp/client.py` (`QgisMCPClient` class) used for direct testing without MCP.

## Commands

```bash
# Run the MCP server (how Claude Desktop launches it)
uv run --no-sync src/qgis_mcp/server.py

# Run with custom host/port
QGIS_MCP_HOST=192.168.1.100 QGIS_MCP_PORT=9877 uv run --no-sync src/qgis_mcp/server.py

# Run against several QGIS instances from one server (tools take instance="b")

# Run with streamable HTTP transport (for remote/multi-client)

# Run with compound tool mode (reduces 118 tools to 27 grouped tools)

# Run the multi-client installer (plugin symlink + MCP client config)

# Run unit tests (no QGIS needed - mocked socket)

# Run integration tests (requires QGIS plugin server running on localhost:9876)

```

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `QGIS_MCP_HOST` | `localhost` | Host for QGIS plugin socket connection |
| `QGIS_MCP_PORT` | `9876` | Port for QGIS plugin socket connection |

## MCP Tools, Resources, Prompts, Protocol Features
